outcome: I can calculate PED from data, explain how PED affects total revenue, and use HINTS to explain why demand is elastic or inelastic.

learn.text:
[[Price elasticity of demand]] (PED) measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price.

**PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price**, where [[percentage change]] = (new − original) ÷ original × 100.

PED is usually negative, because price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. We judge its size without the minus sign. More than 1 is [[price elastic]]. Less than 1 is [[price inelastic]]. Exactly 1 is [[unitary PED]].

[[Total revenue]] (TR) = price × quantity. When a firm raises its price, two forces pull on TR. The **price pull**: every cup still sold earns more. The **quantity pull**: cups no longer sold earn nothing. If demand is elastic, the quantity pull is bigger, so a price rise **lowers** TR. If demand is inelastic, the price pull is bigger, so a price rise **raises** TR.

How elastic demand is depends on the [[determinants of PED]]. We use [[HINTS]]: **H**abits, **I**ncome share, **N**ecessity, **T**ime and **S**ubstitutes.
learn.caption: The price rises from P₁ ($6) to P₂ ($7). Cups sold fall from Q₁ (160) to Q₂ (120). The price pull (hatched) adds $120. The quantity pull (cross pattern) loses $240. TR falls from $960 to $840, so demand is price elastic here.

try.intro:
**Welcome to your café**. Each day, choose a price and open the café. Watch how many customers come in and your [[total revenue]]. The demand curve is **hidden** until the end of the week. Other things stay the same all week ([[ceteris paribus]]).

**Level 1:** each week, finish with more daily revenue than on day 1 **and** decide correctly whether demand is price elastic or price inelastic. Do both in 3 of the 4 weeks to earn the **Café Tycoon** stamp.

**Level 2:** these price ranges cross the point where |PED| = 1. Find the price that earns the most revenue.

**Level 3:** only five days, and you work out each PED yourself before the sales log shows it.

scenarios.name: Latte on Market Street
scenarios.text: You sell lattes on a busy street. There are **five other cafés** within one block.

hints.text: Some customers have a daily latte habit, which makes demand a little less elastic.
One latte is a small part of income. On its own, this makes demand less elastic.
A latte is a want, not a need. People can easily go without one.
Customers can switch café right away. It takes no time to walk next door.
Five other cafés sell lattes nearby. Many close substitutes is the strongest factor here, so demand is price elastic.

scenarios.name: Hot chocolate at the ski lodge
scenarios.text: You sell hot chocolate in the **only lodge** at the top of a ski hill. The next café is at the bottom, 20 minutes away by chairlift.

hints.text: A hot chocolate after a cold run is a habit for many skiers.
It is a small part of what skiers spend that day. The lift pass costs far more.
Cold, tired skiers feel it is close to a need at that moment.
Skiers want a drink now. They have no time to look for something else.
There are no close substitutes at the top of the hill. So demand is price inelastic.

scenarios.name: Mystery: the Cloud Fizz
scenarios.text: You sell a new sparkling fruit drink called the **Cloud Fizz** at a weekend market. Is demand elastic or inelastic? Find out from your sales.

hints.text: The drink is new, so nobody has a habit of buying it yet.
One drink is a small part of income, but this alone does not make demand inelastic.
A fancy fruit drink is a luxury, not a necessity.
Shoppers can walk to another stall in a minute.
The market has many drink stalls with juice, lemonade and water. Many substitutes make demand price elastic.

scenarios.name: Mystery: the platform kiosk
scenarios.text: You run the **only coffee kiosk** on a busy train platform. It is 6:30 in the morning and the next train leaves in five minutes. Is demand elastic or inelastic? Find out from your sales.

hints.text: Many commuters buy a coffee every morning. It is a strong habit.
One coffee is a small part of a commuter's income.
Tired commuters feel they need a coffee to start the day.
The train leaves in five minutes. There is no time to look for another seller.
There is no other coffee on the platform, so there are no close substitutes. Demand is price inelastic.

scenarios.name: Smoothie bar at the gym
scenarios.text: Gym members buy smoothies after a workout. You start at a low price. Find the price that earns the most in a day.

scenarios.name: Bubble tea near the school
scenarios.text: Students walk past after school. You start at a high price. Find the price that earns the most in a day.

scenarios.name: Soup from a food truck
scenarios.text: Office workers buy lunch from your truck. Find the price that earns the most in a day.

scenarios.name: Coffee at the ferry dock
scenarios.text: Only five days this week. Work out each PED yourself.

scenarios.text: Only five days this week. Work out each PED yourself.

decision.typeQuestion: In this price range, is demand for your drink price elastic or price inelastic?
decision.moveQuestion: To raise total revenue, should the café raise or lower its price?

feedback.typeRight: Yes. Demand is **price {type}** in this price range.
feedback.typeWrong: Not this time. Demand is **price {type}** in this price range. Look at your own data below to see why.
feedback.example: On Day {day} you changed the price from {p1} to {p2} ({pctP}). Cups sold changed from {q1} to {q2} ({pctQ}). PED = {pctQ} ÷ {pctP} = **{ped}**. The size of PED is **{compare} 1**, so quantity demanded changed by a {bigger} percentage than price.
feedback.pattern: Across the week, your PED values averaged **{mean}** (without the minus sign). In {opposite} of your {changes} price changes, total revenue moved the **opposite** way to price. In {same}, it moved the **same** way as price.
feedback.noData: You kept the same price all week, so there is no PED to calculate from your data. Next week, change the price on some days and compare.
feedback.moveRight: Yes. To raise total revenue, the café should **{move}** its price.
feedback.moveWrong: Not this time. To raise total revenue, the café should **{move}** its price.
feedback.whyElastic: Demand is elastic, so when the price rises, the quantity pull (revenue lost on cups no longer sold) is bigger than the price pull (extra revenue on cups still sold). A price cut works the other way: the extra cups sold add more revenue than the lower price takes away.
feedback.whyInelastic: Demand is inelastic, so when the price rises, the price pull (extra revenue on cups still sold) is bigger than the quantity pull (revenue lost on cups no longer sold). Customers keep buying, so a higher price brings in more revenue.
feedback.reveal: Here is the hidden demand curve D. Your dots all lie on it.
feedback.hl: ^HL^ PED changes as you move along a straight demand curve. In this price range it goes from {pedLow} at {pLow} to {pedHigh} at {pHigh}, but it stays {side} 1 the whole time.

try.goal: Set a price each day, read your sales log, and grow your revenue.

levels.title: Read your customers
levels.blurb: Four cafés. Grow revenue and decide: elastic or inelastic?

sweet.question: Along a straight demand curve, where is total revenue highest?

options.elastic: Where demand is price elastic (|PED| more than 1)
options.inelastic: Where demand is price inelastic (|PED| less than 1)

sweet.right: Yes. Total revenue is highest where |PED| = 1.
sweet.wrong: Not this time. Total revenue is highest where |PED| = 1.
sweet.reached: Your best day was Day {day} at {price}, with total revenue {best}. The most this café can earn in a day is {max}, at {maxPrice}. You reached {pct}% of it. The goal was {goal}%.
sweet.why: Below {maxPrice}, demand is price inelastic, so a higher price raises total revenue. Above {maxPrice}, demand is price elastic, so a higher price lowers total revenue. At {maxPrice}, |PED| = 1, so a small price change leaves total revenue almost the same.
sweet.pedHelp: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Use Day {prev} as the original value. Round to 2 decimal places.
sweet.pedWrong: Not quite. Check which day is the original value, then try again.
sweet.hl: ^HL^ PED changes as you move along a straight demand curve. Here it goes from {pedLow} at {pLow} to {pedHigh} at {pHigh}. |PED| = 1 at {maxPrice}, the midpoint of the curve.

try.nickname: "Price pull" and "quantity pull" are this app's nicknames. In an exam, write "the extra revenue from the higher price on units still sold" and "the revenue lost on units no longer sold".

check.prompt: A food truck raises the price of a taco from **$4.00 to $5.00**. Quantity demanded falls from **200 to 170** tacos a day. Calculate the PED. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

mistakes.feedback: You divided % change in price by % change in quantity. The formula is the other way up: PED = % change in **quantity demanded** ÷ % change in **price**.
You used the new values ($5.00 and 170) as the base. Percentage change uses the **original** values: (new − original) ÷ original × 100.
You divided the change in quantity (−30) by the change in price ($1). PED uses **percentage** changes, not the raw changes.
The size is right, but price and quantity demanded moved in opposite directions, so PED is **negative**.

hints: Work out the two percentage changes first, then divide.
% change in price = (5 − 4) ÷ 4 × 100. % change in quantity = (170 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100.
check.worked: Example with different numbers: price rises from $2.00 to $2.50, so % change in price = 0.50 ÷ 2.00 × 100 = +25%. Quantity falls from 100 to 90, so % change in quantity = −10 ÷ 100 × 100 = −10%. PED = −10 ÷ 25 = −0.4.
check.explanation: % change in price = (5 − 4) ÷ 4 × 100 = +25%. % change in quantity demanded = (170 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = −15%. PED = −15 ÷ 25 = **−0.6**. Its size is less than 1, so demand is price inelastic.

check.prompt: The PED for school bus passes is **−0.3**. What does this tell you?

options.text: Demand is price inelastic: a 10% price rise lowers quantity demanded by about 3%
options.feedback: Yes. The minus sign shows price and quantity move in opposite directions. The size, 0.3, is less than 1, so quantity responds by a smaller percentage than price.

options.text: Demand is price elastic, because PED is negative
options.feedback: The minus sign only shows direction. Almost every PED is negative. To judge elastic or inelastic, look at the size: 0.3 is less than 1.

options.text: A 10% price rise lowers quantity demanded by 30%
options.feedback: That would be a PED of −3. Use the rearranged formula: % change in quantity = PED × % change in price = −0.3 × 10 = −3%.

options.text: A 10% price rise raises quantity demanded by 3%
options.feedback: The size is right, but the sign is negative. A higher price means a **lower** quantity demanded.

hints: Read the sign and the size separately.
Is 0.3 bigger or smaller than 1? What does the minus sign show?
check.worked: Example: PED for phone cases is −2. The size, 2, is more than 1, so demand is price elastic. A 5% price rise lowers quantity demanded by 2 × 5 = 10%.
check.explanation: The sign shows direction (opposite ways). The size shows how strongly quantity responds. |−0.3| = 0.3 is less than 1, so demand is price inelastic: a 10% price rise gives about a 3% fall in quantity demanded.

check.prompt: Demand for films at a cinema has a PED of **−1.8**. The cinema raises its price. What happens to its [[total revenue]]?

options.text: Total revenue falls
options.feedback: Yes. Demand is elastic, so quantity falls by a bigger percentage than price rises. The quantity pull is bigger than the price pull.

options.text: Total revenue rises
options.feedback: That happens when demand is **inelastic**. Here |PED| = 1.8, which is more than 1, so the lost sales cost more revenue than the higher price brings in.

options.text: Total revenue stays the same
options.feedback: TR stays the same only when PED is unitary (exactly 1 in size). Here it is 1.8.

options.text: You cannot tell without knowing the cinema's costs
options.feedback: Total revenue is price × quantity. It does not depend on costs, so PED is enough to answer.

hints: When demand is elastic, which pull is bigger: the price pull or the quantity pull?
check.worked: Example: a gym has PED = −0.5 and raises its fee by 10%. Members fall by only 5%, so the price pull is bigger and total revenue rises.
check.explanation: |PED| = 1.8 is more than 1, so demand is price elastic. A price rise lowers quantity demanded by a bigger percentage, so total revenue falls. To raise revenue, the cinema should lower its price instead.

check.prompt: The PED for bread in a town is **−0.4**. A bakery raises its price by **10%**. Calculate the percentage change in quantity demanded.

mistakes.feedback: You divided 10 by 0.4. Rearrange the formula: % change in quantity = PED × % change in price.
You divided 10 by 0.4. Rearrange the formula: % change in quantity = PED × % change in price.
Your working is right, but the answer is a percentage. −0.4 × 10 = −4, so the answer is −4%, not −0.04.
The size is right, but a higher price means quantity demanded **falls**. The answer should be negative.

hints: Rearrange PED = % change in Qd ÷ % change in P.
% change in Qd = PED × % change in P.
check.worked: Example: PED for concert seats is −2. The price falls by 5%. % change in Qd = −2 × −5 = +10%. Quantity demanded rises by 10%.
check.explanation: % change in quantity demanded = PED × % change in price = −0.4 × 10 = **−4%**. Demand for bread is inelastic, so quantity falls by less than price rises.

check.prompt: Use [[HINTS]]. Which product is likely to have the **most price inelastic** demand?

options.text: Insulin for a person with diabetes
options.feedback: Yes. It is a necessity (N) with no close substitutes (S), so people keep buying it even when the price rises.

options.text: One brand of sports drink
options.feedback: There are many other brands of sports drink. Many close substitutes (S) make demand for one brand elastic.

options.text: A holiday cruise
options.feedback: A cruise is a luxury, not a necessity (N), and it takes a big share of income (I). Both make demand more elastic.

options.text: A film at the cinema on a Friday night
options.feedback: People can watch a film at home, go bowling or see friends. Many substitutes (S) make demand fairly elastic.

hints: Go through H, I, N, T, S for each product.
Which product is a necessity and has no close substitute?
check.worked: Example: compare petrol for a commuter with no bus service, and one brand of chocolate bar. Petrol is a necessity with no close substitutes for that person, so its demand is more inelastic than one brand of chocolate.
check.explanation: Insulin is a necessity with no close substitutes. People with diabetes need it whatever the price. So its demand is very price inelastic. The other products all have substitutes or are luxuries.

check.prompt: Fuel prices rise. In the first month, drivers buy almost the same amount of fuel. After two years, many have switched to electric bikes and buses, and fuel sales have fallen a lot. Which HINTS determinant explains this best?

options.text: Time
options.feedback: Yes. Over a longer time, people find and switch to substitutes, so demand becomes more price elastic.

options.text: Habits
options.feedback: Habits make demand **less** elastic. The key change here is that people had **time** to find alternatives.

options.text: Income share
options.feedback: The share of income spent on fuel did not change much between the first month and two years later. What changed was the time to adjust.

options.text: Necessity
options.feedback: Fuel was a necessity in both periods. The difference is that, given time, people found other ways to travel.

hints: What is different between the first month and two years later?
Think about how long people need to find another way to travel.
check.worked: Example: when the price of home heating oil rises, families cannot change their heating system in a week. After a few years, many install heat pumps. Demand for oil is more elastic in the long run.
check.explanation: The longer the time period, the more price elastic demand becomes, because consumers have time to find substitutes and change their behaviour.

check.prompt: A café sells **300 cups** of tea a week at **$5.00**. PED for its tea is **−1.5**. The café raises its price by **10%** to **$5.50**. Calculate its **new total revenue**.

mistakes.feedback: You made quantity **rise** by 15%. A price rise lowers quantity demanded: −1.5 × 10 = −15%.
You divided 10 by 1.5. Use % change in Qd = PED × % change in P = −1.5 × 10 = −15%.
You used a 1.5% fall in quantity. PED × % change in price = −1.5 × 10 = −15%, so quantity falls by 15%, not 1.5%.
You found the new quantity (255), but multiplied it by the old price. Use the new price, $5.50.
That is the **change** in total revenue. The question asks for the **new** total revenue.
$1,500 is the old total revenue (300 × $5.00). Find the new quantity first.

hints: First find the % change in quantity demanded, then the new quantity.
% change in Qd = −1.5 × 10 = −15%. New quantity = 300 × 0.85. New TR = new price × new quantity.
check.worked: Example with different numbers: 200 cups at $4.00, PED = −0.5, price rises 20% to $4.80. % change in Qd = −0.5 × 20 = −10%, so 180 cups. New TR = $4.80 × 180 = $864 (up from $800).
check.explanation: % change in Qd = −1.5 × 10 = −15%. New quantity = 300 × 0.85 = 255 cups. New TR = $5.50 × 255 = **$1,402.50**. Old TR was $1,500, so TR fell by $97.50, as expected for elastic demand.

check.prompt: A government wants to put an [[indirect tax]] on one product to **raise as much tax revenue as possible**. Which product should it choose, and why?

options.text: Cigarettes, because demand is price inelastic, so quantity falls only a little and the tax is collected on many units
options.feedback: Yes. Smokers have strong habits (H) and few substitutes (S), so sales stay high and the government collects tax on most of them.

options.text: Restaurant meals, because demand is price elastic, so the price rises a lot
options.feedback: With elastic demand, quantity falls a lot when the tax raises the price. Fewer units are sold, so the government collects less tax.

options.text: Any product, because PED does not affect tax revenue
options.feedback: Tax revenue = tax per unit × units sold. PED decides how far units sold fall, so it matters a lot.

options.text: One brand of bottled water, because it is a necessity
options.feedback: Water is a necessity, but **one brand** has many close substitutes. Buyers switch to other brands, so demand for it is elastic.

hints: Tax revenue = tax per unit × number of units sold.
For which product will the number of units sold fall the least when the price rises?
check.worked: Example: a $1 tax on a good with inelastic demand cuts sales from 1,000 to 950 units, so tax revenue = $950. The same tax on a good with elastic demand cuts sales from 1,000 to 600, so tax revenue = $600.
check.explanation: Governments raise more tax revenue from goods with price inelastic demand, because quantity falls only a little after the tax. This is why many governments tax cigarettes, alcohol and fuel. Firms use PED in the same way when they set prices.

check.prompt: A café raises its price from P₁ to P₂. **Label the revenue areas.** Choose what each letter shows.

diagram.title: A demand curve with total revenue split into three lettered areas
diagram.description: A demand curve. The price rises from $6 to $7 and quantity falls from 160 to 120 cups. Area A is the thin strip from $6 to $7 over 0 to 120 cups. Area B is the strip from 120 to 160 cups below $6. Area C is the rectangle from 0 to 120 cups below $6.

slots.answer: Revenue gained: the higher price on cups still sold
slots.feedback: A is the price rise ($1) times the cups still sold (120). This is revenue gained.

slots.answer: Revenue lost: cups no longer sold
slots.feedback: B is the 40 cups no longer sold, times the old price ($6). This is revenue lost.
C is the 120 cups sold at both prices, times $6. The café earns this before and after the change.

choices: Revenue gained: the higher price on cups still sold
Revenue lost: cups no longer sold
hints: Total revenue is a rectangle: price times quantity.
Compare the TR rectangle at P₁ with the one at P₂. Which part is in both? Which part is only in one?
check.worked: Example: a cinema raises tickets from $10 to $12 and sells 80 instead of 100. Revenue gained: $2 × 80 = $160. Revenue lost: 20 × $10 = $200. Revenue kept: $10 × 80 = $800. TR falls by $40, so demand is price elastic here.
check.explanation: **A** = $1 × 120 = $120 gained. **B** = 40 × $6 = $240 lost. **C** = $6 × 120 = $720 kept. B is bigger than A, so total revenue falls by $120. Demand is **price elastic** over this range (in the app, A is the "price pull" and B is the "quantity pull").

explain.prompt: Explain, using your sales log, whether demand for your café's drink was price elastic or price inelastic, and what the café should do to raise its total revenue.
frames: On Day ___, I changed the price from ___ to ___, and cups sold changed from ___ to ___.
The PED was ___, which is ___ than 1 in size, so demand is price ___.
When I raised the price, total revenue ___ because the ___ pull was bigger.
Demand was ___ because of HINTS, especially ___.
checklist: I used real numbers from my sales log (prices and cups sold).
I calculated PED and compared its size with 1.
I said what happened to total revenue and linked it to PED.
I said whether the café should raise or lower its price, and gave a HINTS reason.

teacherNotes: Each scenario has a hidden straight-line demand curve. Its playable price range lies wholly on the elastic part (latte, Cloud Fizz) or wholly on the inelastic part (ski lodge) of the line, so every price change the student makes gives the same answer. Cups sold are whole numbers and every PED in the sales log is worked out from them, using the previous day as the original value. The price pull is the price change on the units sold at both prices: (P₂ − P₁) × the smaller quantity. The quantity pull is the units gained or lost, valued at the lower price: lower price × (Q₂ − Q₁). The two areas never overlap, and together they equal the change in TR. In class: give half the room the latte and half the ski lodge, then compare their sales logs and link the results to HINTS. You can edit the scenarios (demand points, price range, start price, axes and HINTS text) in this file; keep each price range on one side of the unitary point, which the automated tests check. PED changing along a straight line is HL, and is labelled HL in the reveal.
